title: The Last Train
author: Ahmed Al-Qashar
subtitle: An Adventure Story
synopsis: Daniel takes the last train to Lakeview to visit his sister. Outside, the rain is strong and the mountains are dark. Then he finds a brown bag under a seat. Inside is an important warning about the old river bridge. Daniel, the conductor, and a quiet stranger must work together before the train reaches the bridge.

chapters.title: The Last Platform
paragraphs: On a wet Friday evening, Daniel Ellis stood at Riverford Station.
He was twenty-three years old. He had one small case and a blue ticket. He was going to Lakeview to see his sister, Emily. He had not seen her for six months.
The station was almost empty. A yellow lamp shone above the door. Rain ran down the glass windows. A large round clock showed ten thirty. The last train was due to leave at ten forty-five.
Daniel looked at the dark rails. Beyond the station, he could see the mountains. The clouds were low over the hills. There was a cold wind, and the trees moved from side to side.
An old man sat on a bench near the clock. A woman carried a basket to the train. Two railway workers walked past with a lamp. Nobody spoke loudly. The evening was quiet, except for the rain.
A long train came slowly into the station. Its black engine made a deep sound. White steam rose into the cold air. Light came from the windows of the carriages. Daniel was glad to see it.
A conductor in a dark coat stood by the first carriage. His name was Mr Harris. He had a silver watch in one hand and a ticket book in the other. He smiled at Daniel.
'Lakeview?' Mr Harris asked. Daniel showed his ticket. 'Yes. My sister is waiting for me.' The conductor looked at the sky. 'It may be a slow journey tonight,' he said.
'Because of the rain?' Daniel asked. 'Because of the rain and the river,' Mr Harris answered. 'The train must go over an old bridge before we reach Lakeview.'
Daniel looked toward the mountains again. He knew the bridge. When he was a child, he and Emily had watched trains cross it from a hill near their home. The bridge looked small from far away.
A man in a grey coat walked quickly along the platform. He had a hat low over his eyes. He looked into each carriage, then stopped beside the last door. Daniel thought he was looking for someone.
The man turned and saw Daniel watching him. For one second, his face looked worried. He opened his mouth to speak, but the train gave a loud whistle. The man stepped away.
'All aboard!' called Mr Harris. Daniel picked up his case and went inside. He found a window seat in the second carriage. Outside, the platform lamps shone on the wet stones.
The engine moved. The station clock passed slowly behind the window. Daniel waved at no one. He was thinking about Emily and the hot supper she had promised him.
The train left the town and entered the dark country. Trees passed the windows. The wheels made a steady sound. Daniel put his case on the shelf above his head.
He sat down and opened a small book. But after a minute he closed it again. There was something under the seat opposite him: the corner of a brown leather bag.
It was not his bag. No one was sitting in the seat. Daniel leaned forward. The bag had two strong straps and a little metal lock. A name was written on a white card tied to its handle.
Daniel could read only two words in the weak light: E. SHAW. Under the name were three more words, written in dark red ink: RIVER BRIDGE TWELVE.
The rain grew stronger. Daniel looked at the words once more. The train was going toward the river bridge. He did not know why, but he felt that the bag was important.

chapters.title: The Forgotten Bag
paragraphs: Daniel waited for a few minutes. People in the carriage read newspapers or looked out of the windows. A young couple spoke quietly. No one asked about the brown bag.
He looked at the white name card again. Its string was wet, as if the bag had stood in the rain. A small piece of paper was caught under one strap. Daniel could see black letters on it.
He did not open the bag. It belonged to another person. Instead, he stood up and went to find Mr Harris. The conductor was checking tickets in the next carriage.
'Excuse me,' Daniel said. 'There is a bag under an empty seat. I think someone left it there.' Mr Harris put away his ticket book and followed him.
The conductor bent down beside the bag. 'A railway worker's bag,' he said. 'That looks like an old company tag.' He read the name aloud. 'E. Shaw.'
'Do you know him?' asked Daniel. 'I know a man called Ernest Shaw,' said Mr Harris. 'He works near the river. But I have not seen him today.'
Mr Harris lifted the paper from under the strap. It was folded in four. He opened it carefully. Across the top were the words: CHECK BRIDGE TWELVE BEFORE THE LAST TRAIN.
There was a simple drawing below the words. It showed a bridge and the river under it. One part of the bridge had a large black cross on it. Beside the cross was the word BROKEN.
Daniel felt cold. 'Is that our bridge?' he asked. 'Yes,' Mr Harris said. He read the paper again. Then he looked out at the rain. 'I must speak to the driver.'
A man came to the door between the carriages. He wore a grey coat and a dark hat. Daniel knew the man from the station. The man looked at the bag, then at Mr Harris.
'Is that bag yours?' Mr Harris asked. The man did not answer at once. 'I know that bag,' he said at last. 'Please tell me where you found it.'
'Under this seat,' said Daniel. 'Who are you?' The man took off his hat. His hair was grey at the sides. He looked tired. 'My name is Thomas Shaw,' he said.
'Are you Ernest Shaw?' asked Mr Harris. 'No. Ernest is my brother.' Thomas looked at the paper in the conductor's hand. 'That is his writing. Has something happened at the bridge?'
Mr Harris folded the note. 'We do not know yet,' he said. 'But we will check. Please stay here while I speak to the driver.' He put the bag safely beside his chair.
Thomas sat down slowly. Daniel sat opposite him. The wheels made their steady sound, but neither man spoke. Outside, the rain fell across the dark fields.
At last Thomas said, 'My brother left home very early this morning. He was going to the bridge. He said he had to check something after the storm.'
'The storm was last night?' Daniel asked. Thomas nodded. 'The river is very high. Ernest does not like that old bridge when the water is high.'
Daniel looked at the paper and the black cross. He had wanted a simple journey to Lakeview. Now he wondered if the train was moving toward danger.

chapters.title: A Warning on the Map
paragraphs: Mr Harris went along the moving train to the engine. He held the folded note inside his coat so that it would stay dry. The driver, Mr Bell, listened carefully while the train ran through the hills.
'There is a warning about Bridge Twelve,' the conductor said. 'I want us to stop at Glenbrook Station and ask for news.' The driver looked at the note and then at the dark line ahead.
'We have a green signal,' Mr Bell said. 'But a green signal does not tell us what the river is doing. We can stop at Glenbrook. It is before the bridge.'
Mr Harris thanked him. He went back to the carriages. For the first time that night, Daniel heard the engine make a long, low whistle. The train began to move more slowly.
In the second carriage, Thomas still sat beside the brown bag. His hands were closed. He watched every door. When Mr Harris returned, he stood up quickly.
'We are going to stop before the bridge,' Mr Harris told him. 'Do you have anything that can help us?' Thomas thought for a moment. 'There may be a map in the side pocket of the bag,' he said.

Mr Harris opened the small outside pocket. A flat paper lay inside. It had no private letter on it. It was a map of the railway from Riverford to Lakeview. The names of the stations were easy to read.
A thick red line showed the river. A short black line showed the bridge. Beside it were the same words: BRIDGE TWELVE. A small arrow pointed to the north side of the bridge.
'What does the arrow mean?' Daniel asked. Thomas touched the paper. 'Ernest and I used to work on the railway together,' he said. 'I think he wants someone to look at that side.'
'But why is the name E. Shaw on the bag?' Daniel asked. Thomas gave a small smile. 'Because Ernest never buys a new bag. This old one was our father's.'
The conductor kept the map on the table in front of them. He did not put it away. Every few minutes he read the warning again. Daniel could see a small mark near the corner of the paper.
The mark looked like a number: 6. Beside it were two short words, partly washed away by the rain. Thomas leaned close. 'Six in the evening,' he said. 'That is when Ernest finished his last check.'
'He checked the bridge today?' Daniel asked. 'It looks that way,' said Mr Harris. 'But we need to hear from him or from another
A woman near the window was listening. She asked if there was a problem. Mr Harris spoke calmly. 'We have a report to check. We will stop at the next station. Please remain seated.'
The woman nodded. Daniel saw that calm words could help people feel safe. He was glad Mr Harris had not ignored the note or the map.
The train passed a small farm. A light burned in one window. Beyond it, the mountain road disappeared into the rain. Daniel tried to see the river but could not.
Then a bell sounded in the carriage. A lamp above the door moved gently. The train went around a long turn, and the lights of Glenbrook came into view.
Mr Harris stood with the map in his hand. 'We are nearly there,' he said. 'Whatever the warning means, we will find out before we cross that bridge.'

chapters.title: The Man in the Next Car
paragraphs: The train stopped at Glenbrook, a small station between two high hills. Only one lamp burned on the platform. Rain fell from the roof in long lines. There were no people waiting for the train.
Mr Bell stayed in the engine. He sent a railway worker to the station office. The worker tried to send a message to the next station, but the old wire did not work.
'The storm has broken the line,' the worker said when he returned. 'We cannot ask Lakeview for news.' Mr Harris looked toward the hills. 'Then we must wait,' he said.
Daniel watched Thomas walk to the window. The man looked worried, but he did not look angry. Daniel wanted to know more about him. He was not sure why Thomas had been searching the train.
'Why were you looking into the carriages at Riverford?' Daniel asked him. Thomas turned slowly. 'I was looking for Ernest,' he said. 'He was due to travel on this train.'
'But he did not get on,' said Daniel. 'I know,' Thomas answered. 'He called at my house this morning. He asked me to meet him here, near the bridge. Then his friend said he had gone back to work.'
'So you took the train to find him?' Daniel asked. 'Yes. And when I saw his bag, I became afraid. He never leaves his tools behind.'

Mr Harris came back into the carriage. He held a lantern and a dry coat. 'There is an old railway shed beyond the platform,' he said. 'Ernest sometimes works there. I will ask the station worker to check it.'
Thomas rose. 'Can I go with him?' 'You can come as far as the station office,' Mr Harris said. 'But please do not go onto the line. It is dark, and the ground is wet.'
The three men stepped onto the platform. The cold air smelled of rain and smoke. Daniel could hear water running somewhere below the station wall. Thomas looked down the empty track.
Inside the office, a small stove gave off heat. A table held a lamp, a cup, and an open book. The station worker was reading old messages. He looked up when Mr Harris entered.
'Is there any word from Ernest Shaw?' Mr Harris asked. The worker shook his head. 'Not tonight. But there is a note in the book from this afternoon.'
He turned the book toward them. The note said: SHAW AT BRIDGE 12. CHECK NORTH SIDE. RETURN BEFORE
DARK. Under the words was the time: 4:15.
'That is his work,' Thomas said quietly. His finger rested on his brother's name. 'He was there today. We must find him.'
Mr Harris asked the station worker to send two men along the safe service path to the small shed. They had strong lamps and knew the road. They did not need to go onto the bridge.
Daniel stayed in the warm office with Thomas. In the silence he heard the station clock tick. He thought about Emily waiting at Lakeview. He wanted to tell her that he was safe.
After twenty minutes, a light moved outside. One of the railway workers came back alone. His coat was wet, and he carried a small blue notebook.
'We found this in the shed,' he said. 'And we found a message on the door. It says: DO NOT SEND THE TRAIN.'

chapters.title: The Bridge in the Rain
paragraphs: Mr Harris read the message twice. Thomas put his hands on the office table. 'Ernest wrote that,' he said. 'He always uses large letters when the news is important.'
'Where is he now?' asked Daniel. The worker did not know. 'There is a path from the shed to the river,' he said. 'He may be checking the bridge with the other men.'
Mr Bell came into the office. He had stopped the engine safely and asked the passengers to stay warm in the carriages. He looked at the notebook and the map. 'We will not move,' he said.
The station worker opened the notebook. A page showed a drawing of the bridge. The north side had three wooden parts under the rails. One of the parts was marked with a large black circle.
There were words under the drawing: WOOD MOVES. RIVER VERY HIGH. STOP TRAINS. The last line was clear and dark, as if the pen had pressed hard on the paper.
Daniel remembered the old bridge from his childhood. He had never thought about the wood beneath the rails. A bridge could look strong from above and still have a problem below.
'If the wood moves, the train must not cross,' Mr Bell said. He put the notebook beside the map. 'It is good that we stopped. Now we will wait for the railway workers.'
A little later, two lamps appeared beyond the station gate. Three men came up the safe road from the river. Their boots were covered in mud. One of them carried a red flag.
Thomas ran a few steps toward them, then stopped. 'Ernest!' he called. The man with the red flag looked up. He was tall and tired, with a dark coat and wet hair.
'Thomas?' the man said. 'What are you doing here?' Thomas took his brother's hand. For a moment neither spoke. Then Ernest looked past him and saw the waiting train.
'Did it cross the bridge?' Ernest asked quickly. 'No,' Mr Harris answered. 'We stopped here because of your note.' Ernest closed his eyes for a second. 'Thank you,' he said.
The other workers told them what they had seen. The river was very high. One large piece of wood had moved under the bridge. It could not hold a train that night.
'We placed a red flag on the safe side of the line,' Ernest said. 'We tried to send news by the wire, but it was broken. Then I left a message at the shed.'
'Your bag was on the train,' Daniel said. Ernest looked surprised. 'My bag? I put it under a seat at Riverford. I got off to speak to a station worker. Then the train left without me.'
'So you came by the road?' Mr Harris asked. 'Yes,' Ernest said. 'A driver brought me back to the bridge. I did not know my bag was still on the train. The warning paper was inside the strap.'
'I found it,' Daniel said. Ernest turned to him. 'Then you helped stop the train,' he answered. 'You did the right thing when you told the conductor.'
The rain fell softly now. In the quiet station, everyone understood the danger. Nobody had to see the train on the bridge to know that it must stay where it was.
Mr Bell returned to the passengers with clear news: the bridge was closed until the railway could repair it. For tonight, the last train was going no farther.

chapters.title: A Long Night at Glenbrook
paragraphs: The train stood beside the platform. Its lights were warm in the wet night. Mr Harris walked from carriage to carriage and explained why they had stopped. Some passengers were tired. Others were afraid.
'We are safe here,' he told them. 'There is a problem with the old bridge. The railway workers are checking it. We will stay at Glenbrook tonight and travel again when the line is safe.'
The woman with the basket gave a piece of bread to a little boy. An old man shared his newspaper with another passenger. A young woman opened a small book and began to read aloud to her daughter.
Daniel helped Mr Harris carry cups of tea from the station office to the carriages. The tea was hot. The rain was cold. People thanked him as he walked past their seats.
'You do not work for the railway,' Mr Harris said with a smile. 'But tonight you are helping us.' Daniel smiled back. 'I cannot fix a bridge,' he said. 'But I can carry tea.'
Thomas sat beside Ernest in the office. His brother was clean and warm now. The red flag lay on a chair. The brown leather bag stood at Ernest's feet.
'I was afraid when I could not find you,' Thomas said. 'I know,' Ernest answered. 'The work took longer than I thought. I wanted to get the warning to the driver before the train left Riverford.'
'The bag reached him for you,' Thomas said. Ernest shook his head. 'Not by itself. Daniel saw it and spoke up. Mr Harris listened. The driver stopped. Many people made the right choice.'
Daniel sat near the station window and looked at the mountains. He was thinking about his sister. He had promised to be in Lakeview before midnight, and now he would not arrive until morning.
A station worker said he could send a message from the town office. The main wire to Lakeview was broken, but a road worker was going there before daybreak. He could take a short written note.
Daniel wrote: DEAR EMILY, THE TRAIN HAS STOPPED AT GLENBROOK. I AM SAFE. THE OLD BRIDGE NEEDS
WORK. I WILL COME WHEN THE ROAD IS OPEN. LOVE, DANIEL.
The worker put the note in his coat. Daniel thanked him. He felt better. Emily would be worried when the train did not come, but soon she would know why.
At two in the morning, the rain stopped. There were stars over the hills. The station clock made a small sound each hour. Daniel closed his eyes and slept for a short time.
When he woke, a pale light was in the sky. The old hills were blue and grey. Far away, the river moved through the valley. Glenbrook looked different in the morning.
Mr Harris was standing by the train door. 'Good morning,' he said. 'There is news. The bridge is still closed, but a bus can take everyone to Lakeview by the safe mountain road.'
Daniel helped people carry their cases to the bus. Thomas and Ernest said goodbye beside the station gate. Ernest was going back to the bridge with the other railway workers.
'Will the bridge be safe again?' Daniel asked. 'Yes,' Ernest answered. 'But not before we repair it and check it carefully. A train can wait. People cannot be replaced.'
Daniel looked at the quiet train one last time. The engine was cold now. The big lamps were dark. It had been a strange journey, but the train had brought everyone as far as it safely could.

chapters.title: Morning at Lakeview
paragraphs: The bus moved slowly through the mountains. The road was narrow, and the hills were high. Daniel sat by the window. He could see green fields, small houses, and the river far below.
The sun came out between the clouds. There was fresh snow on the highest mountain. Birds flew over the trees. After the long night, the world looked new and quiet.
Mr Harris sat near the front of the bus. He still wore his dark conductor's coat. When the road turned, he looked back to check that everyone was comfortable.
'We are almost there,' he told Daniel. 'The town is just beyond the next hill.' Daniel smiled. 'Thank you for listening to the warning last night,' he said.
'Thank you for bringing it to me,' Mr Harris answered. 'I see many bags on trains. But that bag had an important name and an important message. You did not ignore it.'
The bus came down the last hill into Lakeview. Houses stood near a wide lake. A small church bell rang. Shops were opening. People carried bread and milk along the street.
Emily was waiting near the station with a warm coat in her arms. She saw Daniel through the bus window and waved both hands. Daniel felt a great happiness when he saw her.
He got off the bus and gave his sister a long hug. 'I thought you were lost!' Emily said. 'I was worried all night.' Daniel took her hand. 'I was not lost,' he answered. 'The last train had to stop.'
Emily told him that a road worker had brought his note early that morning. She had read it three times. When she knew Daniel was safe, she made a hot breakfast and came to meet the bus.

They walked to her little house by the lake. Daniel carried his case. Emily asked about the bridge, the bag, and the two brothers. Daniel told her the story slowly, from the station clock to the red flag.
'You were brave,' she said. Daniel shook his head. 'I was only careful. The workers at the bridge were brave. Mr Harris and the driver made good choices. I just found a bag.'
'And you did not leave it under the seat,' Emily said. 'That was important.' Daniel thought about this. A small action could sometimes help many people.
After breakfast, they walked beside the lake. The mountains stood far away in the clear morning air. Daniel could not see the railway bridge, but he knew that the workers were making it safe.
A week later, the railway sent a letter to every passenger. The bridge was repaired and checked. The trains could cross it again. The letter thanked the people who had helped that night.
Daniel put the letter inside his travel book. He kept it next to his blue ticket. The ticket reminded him of the long night, the warm tea, and the people on the train.
On his last evening in Lakeview, Daniel and Emily sat near the water. A train sounded somewhere in the hills. Daniel looked up and smiled. 'I think I will always remember the last train,' he said.
'Because it was late?' Emily asked. 'No,' Daniel answered. 'Because everyone got home safely.' The last light of the day lay on the lake, and for a little while they listened to the distant train.
